query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings, reducing the initial grain size to increase the grain-boundary density will promote the dynamic segregation of Cu during high-temperature sliding. This Cu enrichment at the grain boundaries accelerates the formation of a protective oxide or tribolayer, thereby enhancing wear resistance and reducing microscopic deformation compared to a coarser-grained baseline coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate prepared via a standard processing protocol that results in a relatively coarse grain size (lower grain-boundary density).
generation.intervention: Modify the processing protocol (e.g., via controlled thermo-mechanical treatment or rapid solidification) to produce a finer-grained initial microstructure, thus increasing the grain-boundary density.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in a high-temperature environment at temperatures between 500°C and 700°C that mimic the intended operating regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain-boundary density enabling enhanced dynamic segregation of Cu during high-temperature sliding, leading to the formation and stabilization of a protective oxide/tribolayer.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the finer microstructure provides more active diffusion paths along grain boundaries. This promotes the migration and segregation of low-melting Cu atoms which, in presence of oxygen generated during sliding, form a continuous, protective oxide or tribolayer. This layer minimizes material loss (wear) and limits localized plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline coarse-grained coating, the refined (finer-grained) coating will exhibit reduced wear depth and fewer microscopic deformation features, concomitant with more pronounced Cu segregation at the worn surface and a thicker, more stable oxide/tribolayer.
generation.baseline: Coating with the as-deposited, standard coarse grain size and lower grain-boundary density tested under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis applies specifically under high-temperature sliding conditions (500–700°C). It may not hold under room temperature or static loading conditions where oxidation and dynamic segregation are less prominent.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the grain-boundary density and the rate or extent of Cu segregation and oxide formation remains uncertain. Additionally, contributions from other microstructural factors or elemental interactions cannot be fully ruled out without further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one using the standard processing route (yielding coarse grains) and the other using a modified processing protocol to achieve a significantly finer grain structure. Subject both sets to sliding wear tests at 500–700°C, then analyze wear tracks and microstructural evolution.
measurements: Quantitative wear depth measurements via profilometry
Microscopic imaging (e.g., SEM) for deformation features
Elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to assess Cu segregation at grain boundaries
Thickness and continuity assessment of the oxide/tribolayer (e.g., via XPS or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear depth and microscopic deformation, or if there is no corresponding increase in Cu segregation and protective oxide/tribolayer formation relative to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A single target containing the principal elements, CuMoTaWV, was partially sintered at 1000 °C using SPS to lower the cost and time of target preparation, as shown in Figure 1 . The elemental maps from the cross section of the target in Figure 1 b showed a uniform distribution of all of the elemental phases. This suggests that in the DC sputter film from the single target, the plasma will evaporate all of the principal elements to the substrate. The EDS area analyses from the cross section of the target in Table 2 and Table S1 showed a uniform distribution of elements with slightly lower amounts of Cu and W.

Preparation of a single target of CuMoTaWV: (a) SPS and (b) SEM morphology of the cross section of the target and elemental mapping.

The XRD diffractogram of the CuMoTaWV RHEA film deposited on the 304 stainless-steel substrate is shown in Figure 2 , together with the simulated XRD diffractogram obtained from the DFT-optimized SQS. The as-deposited film showed the formation of a single-phase BCC solid solution with a strong (110) preferred orientation. The experimentally determined lattice parameter is 3.18 Å, which is in good agreement with the one for the DFT-optimized SQS

3.1. Feedstock and SPS Sample Characterisation

The microstructure and morphology of the atomised powder were investigated in cross-sections. The SEM image is shown in Figure 1 a. The single particles exhibit a predominantly spherical shape. A dendritic structure with distinct BSE contrast can be observed, indicating a deviating chemical composition. Due to the high cooling rates during the atomisation process and hence fast solidification, a microstructure with a finer distribution of the phases occurs in comparison to arc-melted samples of the same alloy [ [11] ].

Powder characterisation of AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 feedstock: ( a ) SEM (BSE) cross-section view; ( b ) Cumulative particle size distribution (volume).

The particle size distribution is shown in Figure 1 b. A mean particle size (d50) of 20 µm and a particle size range (−d90 +d10) of −30 +8 µm was determined, showing that despite air classification a high content of very fine particles with a diameter below 20 µm is present in the feedstock. The atomised powder was applied for the production of SPS samples with the mentioned parameters. SEM images of the cross-sections with different magnification are shown in Figure 2 .

frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain and predict how microstructural features in the coating control overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation under sliding at high temperature.
frame.limitation: Current ambiguity about which microstructural/mechanistic feature (grain-boundary behavior, dynamic phase or oxide formation, or segregation effects) predominantly governs wear and deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
constraints: The hypothesis must be single and testable
It requires a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
It must predict directional changes in wear and deformation
It should be valid in the high-temperature sliding regime
It must relate to a mechanistic understanding supported by prior evidence
It must include a specific falsification criterion
frame.regime: Sliding wear tests conducted in a high-temperature environment (e.g., operating at temperatures typical of service conditions, such as 500–700°C)
prior_attempts: Previous studies on traditional alloys and some high-entropy systems have correlated enhanced wear resistance with finer grain sizes, oxide tribolayer formation, or dynamic elemental segregation at grain boundaries. However, these efforts have not isolated a single mechanism in FeNiCrCoCu coatings specifically.

While grain refinement and protective oxide scale formation have been observed separately, a unified, controllable change and its direct influence on sliding wear and deformation at high temperatures have not been conclusively demonstrated.
frame.understanding: It is unknown whether dynamic grain-boundary segregation (especially of Cu) that results in a stable, fine-grained or oxide-enriched surface layer during high-temperature sliding is the primary mechanism governing both wear resistance and microscopic deformation. The hypothesis posits that controlled enhancement of grain-boundary density (e.g., via a modified processing protocol that promotes a finer initial microstructure) enhances segregation-driven stabilization during sliding, thereby reducing wear and limiting deformation.

decision.trend: Earlier work on high-entropy alloy coatings under elevated temperature sliding conditions has demonstrated that wear resistance improvements are associated with microstructural evolution, such as grain size refinement and oxide or tribolayer formation. In one key study (PMC7515071), a powder‐metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA was shown to develop protective scales at high temperature that lowered wear depth, while the interplay between microstructural features and tribological performance was noted. However, these studies did not isolate a single mechanism – for example, the effects of dynamic grain-boundary segregation (e.g., of a low-melting element like Cu) versus other phenomena such as oxidation or phase instability. The trend has moved from correlating overall microstructure with wear performance to attempting more controlled variable studies, but a decisive, single testable hypothesis for the FeNiCrCoCu system remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether increasing grain-boundary density – and the consequent dynamic segregation of Cu during high-temperature sliding – is the dominant mechanism that stabilizes a fine-grained or oxide‐enriched surface, thereby reducing both wear and microscopic deformation. Although prior work hints at benefits from oxide formation and refined microstructures, no controlled study in FeNiCrCoCu has directly linked intentional grain size reduction with enhanced dynamic segregation and improved sliding performance at service temperatures (500–700°C).
decision.lever: Modify the processing protocol to produce a finer initial grain size (hence higher grain-boundary density), thereby promoting dynamic Cu segregation during high-temperature sliding
decision.why: By intentionally controlling the grain size, the experiment will test if enhanced grain-boundary density leads to increased Cu segregation that stabilizes a protective, oxide or tribolayer. This lever directly follows the observed trend from previous studies (e.g., PMC7515071) that suggest refined microstructures improve wear performance, and it directly addresses the gap regarding the dominant mechanistic role of dynamic grain-boundary segregation in FeNiCrCoCu coatings. A falsifying result would be that increasing grain-boundary density does not yield a measurable reduction in wear or microscopic deformation, nor does it correlate with enhanced Cu segregation on the worn surface.
